courses.description: AMHS high school choir is a vocal ensemble open to any student grades 9-12. In this chorus, we develop musical proficiency and literacy through performance of vocal music from across a wide range of musical genres. These ensembles perform at winter and spring concerts, as well as community events on and off campus throughout the school year including Green Mountain Music District, All-State, performance tours, and athletic events.
courses.notes: Vocal Music; Grading: Pass/Fail

courses.description: AMHS high school band is an instrumental ensemble open to any student grades 9-12 who plays or wishes to learn to play a musical instrument. In these ensembles, we develop musical proficiency and literacy through performance of instrumental music across a wide range of musical genres. These ensembles perform at winter and spring concerts, as well as community events on and off campus throughout the school year including Green Mountain Music District, All-State, performance tours, and athletic events. Ensembles rehearse twice weekly.

Students will explore various drawing techniques to help learn about space, proportion, perspective, and how to observe the world around them. It will also explore portraiture. We will use a range of printmaking techniques to execute designs and partner with both school-based and community-based organizations to create actual marketing resources in both digital and printed formats. Entrepreneurial skills will be taught as well as how to be a creative and out-of-the-box thinker! Other 2D media will be explored such as collage and mixed media.

courses.description: Students in this course will work in acrylic paint, oil pastel, and watercolor. With a drawing foundation, students will break down landscapes and apply color theory. Students will explore the history of painting and develop an awareness and appreciation for the work of different artists while practicing various painting techniques to eventually develop their own unique style. Students will work with the elements and principles of art and explore their use in expressing ideas and emotions.

courses.description: This class introduces the student to working with clay. Students will learn several techniques of hand-building and will have the opportunity to throw on the potter’s wheel. Students will focus on independent projects in any medium with the intention of showcasing personal expression and communication through the arts. Students will have the opportunity to display their own work for exhibition.

courses.course_name: Advanced Placement English Literature and Composition
courses.description: The primary goal of this class is to help students become independent thinkers, readers, and writers through college-level material and assignments. The course requirements are aligned with the curricular requirements described in the AP English Literature Course Description. Any students who are willing to put forth the time and effort to meet these requirements may enroll in the class. However, they must rise to meet the requirements of the course. Students engage in close, active reading of a variety of works, ranging in era and genre. All reading assignments include annotating, journalizing, or note-taking. Students are frequently required to participate in and/or lead both small group and whole-class discussions on topics related to their readings. The topics include but are not limited to the way in which literary elements such as diction, detail, imagery, figurative language, syntax, etc., help convey tone which aids in unveiling the work's meaning as a whole. In facilitating the search for the meaning of a work, students are required to acknowledge and discuss the time period in which the work was written and the background of the author. Writing is a major part of the class. The focus is on analytic responses to literature, emphasizing how the author's choices of literary and rhetorical devices (parallel structure, imagery, repetition, allusion, apostrophe, symbolism, figurative language, etc.) convey the work's meaning. However, students also write critical essays in which they support their judgments about a work's social and cultural value. In addition, students write fiction; poetry, both original and imitative; and character pieces in which students assume the voice and point of view of a character from a work of literature. Though the AP Exam is optional, some class time is devoted to exam practice and strategies.
courses.notes: Requirements: Summer reading of four assigned literary works and an essay for each are due the first day of class in the fall.

courses.course_name: English 9/10 College Prep Language Arts and Literacy
courses.description: Students study the different forms and elements that make up both fiction and non-fiction. This study is used as a basis for the introduction of interpretation and analysis. Emphasis is placed on writing and speaking with coherence. The study of grammar and vocabulary is an essential part of the class. Instruction and content are aligned with the Common Core State Standards. Each quarter, two to three weeks will be devoted to familiarizing students with the Smarter Balanced assessment.
courses.prerequisites: Prior year English final course grade of 70 or higher, instructor and school counselor recommendation, and standardized test scores.

courses.course_name: English 9/10 Honors Language Arts and Literacy
courses.description: Students in Honors English, an accelerated college-preparatory course, are introduced to a wide selection of fiction and non-fiction. Emphasis is placed on interpretation and analysis of literary and rhetorical elements. A great deal of attention is given to written analysis. A grammar and vocabulary program is designed to enhance students’ written expression. Students are required to participate in small group and whole class discussions. Because the course is honors level, a greater level of responsibility for and ownership of learning is expected of the students. Instruction and content are aligned with the Common Core State Standards.
courses.prerequisites: Prior year English final course grade of 85 or higher, instructor and school counselor recommendation, and standardized test scores.

courses.description: Students in this course develop reading, writing, listening, and speaking skills through the study of both fiction and non-fiction. Emphasis is placed on the writing process. In addition, students each have an individual learning plan which includes the study of grammar, vocabulary and spelling.

courses.description: This course alternates each year between American literature and British literature. The students develop an awareness of the thematic and social relationship between the writer, the culture, and humanity. Students strive to heighten their awareness of cultural diversity as well as to express in oral and written analyses their critical responses to writers’ work. Emphasis will be placed on further development of effective reading, writing, and critical thinking skills. Grammar, vocabulary, and language skills are integral aspects of the course. Peer review of student work and tests is commonly practiced. Instruction and content are aligned with the Common Core State Standards.

courses.description: The study of literature from Beowulf to contemporary writers involves the understanding of historical context. This course continues the preparation for a successful transition to college. Creative and critical writing, oral presentations, rigorous analytical reading, and critical thinking are particularly stressed. The ability to take effective notes in a lecture setting is further developed. Assessments include weekly written responses, peer revision, quizzes, papers, and tests. Peer review of student work and tests is commonly practiced. Instruction and content are aligned with the Common Core State Standards.

courses.description: Creative Writing introduces students to the four genres of creative writing: creative nonfiction, fiction, poetry, and playwriting. Through reading examples of and writing in these four genres, students will discover that each genre differs greatly in purpose, form, audience, and presentation. They will also see that all four genres share properties endemic to any creative expression. Therefore, a writer should never say they are solely a poet, a novelist, essayist, memoir writer, or playwright.
This course is a continuation of Creative Writing, and involves a more in-depth exploration of writing as creative expression.

courses.course_name: Literature and Film: Classic Stories on Page and Screen
courses.description: Explore the power of storytelling across mediums in this engaging course that pairs classic literature with its most compelling film adaptations. Students will examine how themes, characters, and conflicts translate from page to screen, analyzing what changes, what stays the same, and why these stories continue to resonate. Through discussion, comparison, and critical analysis, students will deepen their understanding of both literature and film as art forms.

Have you ever had a great idea for a product, brand, or business, but didn’t know how to get started? In this class, you’ll learn how to turn your ideas into action through the power of writing and communication, combining entrepreneurial thinking with practical writing skills. You'll build a brand, pitch your vision, and communicate effectively like a professional. Throughout the semester, you’ll develop a business idea, craft compelling written content, and create your website using Google Sites. You’ll write resumes, product descriptions, social media posts, pitch emails, personal bios, and more—all while learning how to tell a story that gets people to listen, click, and invest. The course will also introduce the basics of branding, audience analysis, persuasive techniques, and digital storytelling. Whether you want to start a business, build a personal brand, or just become a sharper, more confident communicator, this course will help you write your way into the real world.

courses.course_name: Senior English Project: Voice, Choice, and Reflection
courses.description: This English course is designed to give students the freedom to explore, create, and express their voice as they prepare for life beyond high school. In Senior Seminar, students choose what matters to them. Through independent projects, self-directed reading, and real-world writing tasks, students will shape their learning journey while developing the communication, critical thinking, and storytelling skills necessary for success in the world ahead. Students will: ● Design and complete independent inquiry projects on topics they care about ● Choose readings that inspire or challenge them ● Write in a variety of genres—college essays, persuasive letters, blog posts, spoken word, op-eds, or podcasts ● Collaborate with peers to share feedback and build a supportive, creative community ● Create a final portfolio that reflects student identity, interests, and growth as writers and thinkers Whether students are preparing for college, career, or creative life, this course will help them take ownership of their ideas and tell their story with power and authenticity.
courses.notes: Final Project: A passion-driven, research-informed, or creative capstone project, along with a curated writing portfolio.

courses.description: This is an elective course that explores how crime and justice are portrayed in media, including news, documentaries, podcasts, social media, and true crime entertainment. Students will examine media bias, misinformation, source credibility, ethical reporting, and the impact media has on public opinion and criminal investigations while building critical thinking and media literacy skills.
This course explores the connections between printed and audiovisual media.

courses.description: The Advanced Placement course in Statistics introduces students to the major concepts and tools for collecting, analyzing and drawing conclusions from data. Students are exposed to four broad conceptual themes: 1. Exploring data: observing patterns and departures from patterns 2. Planning a study: deciding what and how to measure 3. Anticipating patterns in advance: producing models using probability and simulation 4. Statistical inference: confirming models. Students who successfully complete the course are prepared to take the AP examination and may receive credit and/or advanced placement for a first-semester, college-level Introductory Statistics course.

Other topics include: sequences and series, vectors, parametric equations, and polar coordinates. Emphasis is placed on modeling phenomena.

courses.description: The physical education program is designed to provide students with physical activity to help them develop the knowledge and skills necessary to participate in physical activity safely, competently, and with personal satisfaction now and throughout their lives. Physical education is a semester course in which students engage in individual and team sports, physical fitness testing, outdoor education, and cooperative games that provide students with an understanding of personal, lifelong physical fitness and opportunities to be a physically active person for life. All curriculum is designed to meet the National Association for Sport and Physical Education (NASPE) Requirements.

Students will benefit from comprehensive weight training and cardiorespiratory endurance activities. Students will learn the basic fundamentals of strength training, aerobic training, and overall fitness training and conditioning. Students will learn about nutrition, safety, and participation as it applies to physical fitness. Course includes both lecture and activity sessions. Students will be empowered to make wise choices, meet challenges, and develop positive behaviors in fitness, wellness, and movement activity for a lifetime.

This course introduces students to Astronomy, Geology, Mineralogy, and Topography and provides an overview of the geologic and biologic history of the Earth as a complex, dynamic, and evolving planet (earthquakes, volcanism, Plate Tectonics, agents of erosion and deposition).

Students move beyond simple observation to investigate the mechanisms that drive life, from the microscopic interactions within a cell to the complex dynamics of global ecosystems.
courses.fulfills_text: designed to satisfy the biological sciences graduation requirement. The AMHS graduation requirement for science is the successful completion of three (3) years of science (Earth Science and Biology plus one additional year of science electives).

While the foundational units remain the same, Honors students are distinguished by extended content, advanced assessment, and independent research. courses.description: Anatomy and physiology is an exciting inquiry-based science elective in which students investigate the structure, shape, and function of the human body. The course focuses on the relationships and interactions among the organ systems that maintain balance (homeostasis) by responding to internal and external stimuli. Dissections, labs, and case studies are integral to this course. This course is ideal for students interested in human medicine, veterinary science, allied health, and the biological sciences.
courses.notes: Lab component: Students will investigate scientific principles through a comprehensive, inquiry-based laboratory curriculum. This course includes extensive animal dissections. (description continues on p.19)

courses.description: AP Biology provides a rigorous, college-level exploration of the natural world, specifically designed to mirror the introductory curriculum for university biology majors. Moving beyond simple memorization, students cultivate a deep conceptual understanding of life’s governing processes through four "Big Ideas": Evolution, Energetics, Information Storage and Transmission, and Systems Interactions. Through a combination of multimedia resources and an inquiry-based laboratory program that meets College Board requirements, students will investigate key topics including biochemistry, cell structure and communication, genetics, and ecology. This course challenges students to think critically and master advanced lab techniques, effectively preparing them for the AP Exam, offering the chance to earn college credit while exploring how biological systems interact. This course is ideal for students interested in future study in the STEM, biological sciences, and allied health careers.
courses.notes: Lab component: Students will investigate scientific principles through a comprehensive, inquiry-based laboratory curriculum. Summer work: Students must complete a required summer assignment to ensure they are prepared and comfortable with prerequisite content prior to starting the course.

courses.description: This full-year elective course explores the wonder of matter and energy. Students will engage in investigations of the microscopic world of atoms and molecules and the macroscopic properties of chemical systems. Chemistry expands students’ current science knowledge and methods learned in their physical and biological sciences. Emphasis is placed on the strategies needed for critical scientific thinking. Topics include gasses, atomic and nuclear structure, periodic properties, chemical reactions, chemical bonding, molecular structure, intermolecular forces, acids and bases, and electrochemistry. Two separate lab periods a week are part of this course.
courses.credits_text: derived: 1 credit for a full-year course, .5 credit for a semester course
courses.notes: Catalog heading 'Chemistry (Standard & Honors)'

courses.description: This full-year elective course explores motion, forces, and the interactions of matter and energy. Students develop the ability to apply both conceptual and mathematical reasoning to understanding the physical world. Algebraic skill and an understanding of basic trigonometry are important for success, but principles will be represented in non-mathematical models as well. Lab experiments and projects are an integral part of the course as they illustrate the process of scientific discovery. Topics include kinematics, Newtonian motion, light, sound, electricity, and astronomy.

The focus will be to expose students to the design process, research, and analysis of engineering processes. This course will learn the concepts necessary to develop their ideas into solutions that will improve our lives.

courses.description: Food Science explores the fascinating intersection of chemistry, biology, and nutrition through the everyday lens of what we eat. Students investigate how ingredients interact, how cooking transforms food on a molecular level, and how science drives the development of safe, nutritious, and appealing products. Through hands-on labs, sensory evaluations, and small research projects, learners gain practical skills in experimentation, critical thinking, and food preparation. This course is ideal for students curious about culinary arts, health, or STEM fields, and offers a deeper understanding of the science behind the foods we enjoy.
courses.prerequisites: 9th grade science and a willingness to prepare and consume a variety of foods.

courses.description: Materials in Motion invites students to explore how the physical world shapes creative expression. Blending materials science with art studio creations, this course examines how the structure, properties, and behavior of materials influence the way artists design, build, and innovate. Students investigate metals, polymers, ceramics, composites, and emerging smart materials through hands‑on labs and creative projects, learning how factors like strength, flexibility, conductivity, and optical properties open new artistic possibilities.
courses.prerequisites: 9th grade science and a willingness to create and engineer ceramic, glass, and metal designs.

courses.description: Forensic Science explores the fascinating intersection of biology, chemistry, and law through the investigative lens of the modern crime lab. Students investigate how scientists process a crime scene, how physical evidence like DNA can identify a suspect, and how technical data drives the pursuit of justice. Through hands-on labs in blood spatter analysis, toxicology, and mock crime scene investigations, learners gain practical skills in evidence collection and microscopic analysis. As a Flexible Pathway course, students develop key transferable skills in inquiry and communication. A cornerstone of this experience is Professional Field Engagement, where students meet with and interview experts in law enforcement, the legal system, or medical forensics. These interactions allow students to bridge the gap between classroom simulations and the high-stakes reality of criminal justice. This course is ideal for students curious about medical science or law, offering a personalized roadmap for exploring careers in the forensic field.
courses.notes: This course explores mature and sensitive topics, including violent crime, forensic pathology, and crime scene evidence. Students will engage with graphic visual materials and participate in labs involving simulated biological evidence.

courses.description: One Health: Animals, Habitats, and Medicine explores the vital connection between animal healthcare, wildlife management, and global biodiversity. Students investigate the biological needs and welfare of a diverse range of species, from companion pets and equine athletes to livestock and exotic wildlife. Through "medical detective" case studies, learners develop practical skills in physical exams, diagnostic imaging, and health assessments while shifting focus toward holistic animal well-being and ethical care. This Flexible Pathway course prioritizes student agency, allowing individuals to customize their experience through self-directed research or community-based projects—whether they are mastering patient care protocols for veterinary assisting, exploring equine stable management, or collaborating with conservationists on local 20 habitat initiatives. By merging clinical science with advocacy, students build a personalized roadmap toward careers as veterinarians, vet techs, game wardens, or professional animal caretakers.
courses.notes: description continues on p.21

courses.description: This course provides students with a comprehensive understanding of the foundational principles, structures, and processes of American government and political life, focusing on the rights and responsibilities of informed citizenship. Through the exploration of the U.S. Constitution, the Bill of Rights, and key Supreme Court decisions, students will analyze the framework of federalism and the functions of the legislative, executive, and judicial branches. We will examine historical and contemporary political issues, engage in civil discourse, and develop critical thinking skills necessary to evaluate media, participate in the democratic process, and effectively advocate for their beliefs as engaged members of their community and society.

courses.description: This course is designed to provide students with an in-depth look at American history during the twentieth century. Students will study the factors that transformed the United States into a modern nation including economic development, military action, social change, and political ideals. This thematic approach will give students the opportunity to discover the evolution of these factors that have created the country they live in today. Students will read and analyze the text and a variety of primary documents. The course will also emphasize critical thinking, class discussion, and analytical writing.
courses.fulfills_text: A U.S. History course is required for all AMHS students.
courses.notes: Catalog heading 'United States History (Standard & Honors)'. Vermont education regulations require the successful completion of U.S. History for all high school graduates. In addition, Civics is a required course for all AMHS students.

courses.description: This course examines the pivotal events, transformative movements, and profound connections that shaped global society during the 20th century. Beginning with the causes and consequences of World War I, students will trace the rise and fall of totalitarian regimes, the devastating impact of World War II, and the subsequent ideological conflict of the Cold War. The curriculum will also cover critical topics such as decolonization, independence movements in Asia and Africa, the development of modern technology, globalization, and the ongoing struggles for human rights, encouraging students to analyze historical evidence and consider diverse perspectives.

This course will focus on using critical thinking as we look at major, controversial moments in United States History. Prior to the history we will be discussing, we will be taking a deep, analytical look at defining the term “conspiracy theories”, discussing why Americans have become so interested in the concept, and the issues and dangers surrounding belief in these theories. Through reading, writing, watching, and discussing the class will take an analytical look at moments that have changed the United States. Topics will include: the use of spies throughout US History, Aaron Burr’s attempted coup, Confederados, numerous assassinations (MLK/Malcolm X/JFK), Project MK Ultra, Project Paperclip and the use of Nazi and Japanese science after the Second World War, among numerous other issues and complicated events through United States History.

This course was designed to make students think deeply about a wide array of issues in the field of philosophy. The course will provide the students with the historical background of the field of philosophy. Content will include the major historical philosophers and the evolution of philosophical ideas. Students will be engaged in class discussions to evaluate the proposals of past philosophers and to also defend their own views on the major topics. Students will use an online college-level text in order to get the necessary content for the course.

This course was designed to make students think deeply about a wide array of issues in the field of psychology. The course will provide the students with the historical background of the field of psychology. Students will be able to identify notable psychologists from the twentieth century. The class will focus mainly on the the many ways that the field of psychology impacts the individual student. Students will use an online college-level text in order to get the necessary content for the course.

This course will focus on aspects of the law and government in the United States. It will focus on the foundations of law throughout history, including the philosophical foundations and laws within ancient civilizations. Students will then interact with Constitutional, Criminal, and Civil Law in the United States and the impact it has on individuals and groups. Students will interact with secondary and primary sources, movies and documentaries, and a number of projects revolving around the different topics.

This course will look at the history of the United States through the 1960s. We’ll be looking at major political, social, military, and cultural aspects of the time period. Students will be required 22 to read, write, analyze, and discuss numerous aspects of the 1960s through primary sources, secondary sources, and film.

courses.description: This course will study the concept of “exploration” and how it was interpreted by cultures of the past. There will be a focus on cultures throughout human history that have endeavored to explore the world around them. As a class, we will conduct research on these explorative peoples and seek to find the motivations and goals of exploration.

This course will look to instill in students a desire to gain a better understanding of the world around them. Students will study the geography of the world, the US, Vermont, and Arlington. Students will learn the basic principles of features of physical geography. Students will then take their knowledge and understanding of geography to examine the effects of geography on the people and cultures that inhabit the different parts of the world.

This course will look at the history of the United States from the 1900s to modern day with a focus on major eras (Great Depression, Civil Rights Movement, or the War on Terror). The class will require analysis, synthesis, and critical thinking, with approximately 8-10 total films being watched and a 3-5 page paper due for each film. In addition, students may have to watch movies on their own time. The expectation will be that students will understand the context of the films, analyze them for numerous aspects (culture, accuracy, symbolism, etc.), and take part in discussions.

courses.description: This course is designed in order to help students understand and gain additional knowledge about the “Crime with no Name.” This course focuses on understanding the concept and legal definition of Genocide and then researching, discussing, and writing about numerous genocides throughout world history, starting with the Age of Imperialism and moving up through the current day. During each genocide, students will research and discuss the historical context, underlying causes, the history of the event itself, and potential consequences for both the victims and the perpetrators.

courses.description: The American Military History course will analyze the evolution and development of the American military throughout history. Students will study the many wars that have made the United States into the world’s greatest military power. A focus will be the nation’s military leaders and the tactics they developed to go to war. Students will develop skills in analysis, reading, and writing throughout the course.

Investigating population trends, exploring diverse cultural landscapes, and identifying spatial patterns across various scales. From bustling cities to rural areas, you’ll embark on a journey of discovery as you examine the diverse interactions that people have with the environment.

AP U.S. History is a challenging course that is meant to be the equivalent of a first-year college course and can earn students college credit. It is a two-semester survey of American History from the arrival of the first humans in North America to the present. Solid reading and writing skills, along with a willingness to devote considerable time to homework and study, are necessary to succeed. Emphasis is placed on critical and evaluative thinking skills, essay writing, interpretation of original documents, and historiography.

courses.notes: Note: Advanced Placement U.S. History is offered to high school seniors and juniors. AMHS has open enrollment in AP classes and encourages all qualified students to take AP U.S. History. The school recommends that students be earning at least a B in regular social studies courses when they choose the AP U.S. History course. Teacher approval is required.

courses.description: This course is designed to provide the student with skills in decoding and encoding, reading comprehension, grammar and the writing process. Students will have the opportunity to read fiction and non-fiction material, learn and implement writing strategies as well as respond to text through a variety of mediums. This class is based on individual English Language Arts goals and objectives. Progress is monitored through reading probes, spelling assessments and writing sample evaluation. This progress is used to inform ongoing instruction.

This course is designed to address the individual needs of students in the area of mathematics. The students will have an opportunity to learn basic computation skills, problem solving strategies as well as math concepts. The class is based on individual Mathematics goals and objectives. Student progress is monitored though a variety of means and used to inform ongoing instruction.

courses.description: Students are introduced to basic written and conversational Mandarin. Students are encouraged to speak Chinese and engage in performing dialogues and skits in the target language. By the end of the course, students will converse on personal matters, meeting and introducing people, ethnicity and nationality, eating, working, numbers, time expressions and shopping. Students will also be familiar with the foundations of the Chinese writing system including both pinyin Romanization and simplified characters. Through projects, students will learn about Chinese culture, festivals, food and geography. Students will also watch Chinese movies and listen to both traditional and popular Chinese music.

Chinese II is sequential to Chinese I. In this course, students further develop their language skills and cultural understanding. Students will learn how to talk about daily schedules, expressing emotions, currency, describing people and places, occupations, colors, and clothing. Students will research and discuss Chinese painting, opera, and forms of traditional Chinese literature and poetry. In addition to the textbook, we will continue to use films and music as a way of furthering our understanding of Chinese culture. Calligraphy is introduced to help students understand character formation and establish a strong foundation in the Chinese writing system. Students will be taught how to type in Chinese and assigned projects involving computers. Students will keep a journal in Chinese which they will use weekly to help build composition skills.

Chinese III is sequential to Chinese II. This course will help students develop deeper comprehension and the ability to express oneself effectively and appropriately in Chinese. Students will make the transition from sentence level discourse to longer, more nuanced modes of self-expression. Students in Chinese III will use Chinese as their major mode of communication 25 during class. Topics include: making apologies, accepting gifts, discussing a trip, making offerings, talking about classes, and traveling on public transportation. Students in Chinese III will use authentic materials to improve their understanding of the language, and also begin reading short stories and poetry in Chinese in order to build up their character recognition and reading comprehension. Students will keep a journal in Chinese which they will use weekly to help build composition skills. Projects will include learning how to compose letters and cards in Chinese, researching and presenting on festivals, literature, and various other areas of student interest. Students are expected to be able to type short essays in Chinese and present in Chinese to the class on projects and research.
courses.notes: description continues on p.26

courses.description: Chinese IV is sequential to Chinese III. Students in Chinese IV will use Chinese as their major mode of communication during class. Students will watch a movie with a complete film script and be asked to read authentic Chinese stories, poems, newspapers, and other social and cultural forms of the written language. Students will continue to keep a journal and be required to compose essays each week on varying subjects. In preparation for future study of Chinese at the college level, Chinese IV begins to introduce higher-level discourse that students will need to continue to mature in their language abilities. Students will learn to travel, chat with native speakers of Chinese, express opinions, and learn how to express emotions. A heavy emphasis will be placed on practical, colloquial Chinese and more formal professional Chinese writing.

courses.description: This course is taught in English. French is a language that is spoken on 5 continents. In this class students will explore the history, music, geography, food, and modern life in each region we study, including North America (Quebec, Vermont, Louisiana), the Caribbean and South America, Europe, Africa, and Asia. We will look at why French is spoken in that place and the role that it plays today in that society. There is no prerequisite for this class. Much of the same material is covered in French language classes but over several courses, so students should be aware that there is some overlap.
courses.notes: Taught in English. There is no prerequisite for this class.

courses.description: Students are introduced to basic written and conversational French. Students are encouraged to speak French and engage in speaking and writing in the target language. Other topics covered include the countries where French is spoken, popular francophone music, and cultural foods. By the end of the course, students will converse on personal matters, meeting and introducing people, nationality, eating, working, numbers, time expressions and school. Through projects, students will learn about French culture, holidays, food and geography. There is an honors option available to students that students can commit to early in the first semester. In honors French there are additional topics and assignments for which students are responsible, and assessments will include this extra material.

French II is sequential to French I. In this course, students further develop their language skills and cultural understanding. Students will learn how to talk about food, recipes, describing people and places, colors, and different preferences. Students will continue to learn about different Francophone countries around the world. In addition to the textbook, we will continue to use videos and music as a way of furthering our understanding of French culture. There is an honors option available to students that students can commit to early in the first semester. In honors French there are additional topics and assignments for which students are responsible, and assessments will include this extra material.
courses.prerequisites: French I (recommended grade of C or better in French I)

courses.description: French III is sequential to French II. In this course, students further develop their language skills and cultural knowledge. Students will learn how to talk about travel, health, work, occupations, and clothing. Students will research and discuss French art and continue to learn about different Francophone countries around the world. In addition to the textbook, we will continue to use videos and music as a way of furthering our understanding of French culture.
courses.prerequisites: French II (recommended grade of B- or better in French II)
courses.notes: This class is recommended for anyone participating in the French Exchange.

courses.description: The Vermont Dual Enrollment Program offers students the opportunity to take two FREE college courses during high school, beginning in the summer prior to the junior year. Dual Enrollment is available at all of the Vermont state universities and colleges, as well as some Vermont private colleges, online and in-person. Students must work with their school counselor to apply for a Dual Enrollment voucher and coordinate the courses with their AMHS schedule. Transportation to the colleges for in-person classes is the responsibility of the family. More information is available in the AMHS School Counseling Office.
courses.provider: Vermont state universities and colleges and some Vermont private colleges
courses.notes: program; online and in-person

courses.description: The Early College Program offers students the opportunity to spend their last year of high school entirely on a college campus. The courses are free, but families may be responsible for some fees. Students must apply for this program early and work with their school counselor to make sure all high school graduation requirements are met. Students spend their senior year taking only college courses. At the end of the senior year, students receive an AMHS diploma and walk with their class at graduation, having a full year of tuition-free college completed. Early College is offered at seven Vermont state and private colleges. More information is available in the AMHS School Counseling Office.
courses.notes: program

courses.description: A Work Study may be offered to eligible high school students. Students can earn high school elective credit based on the number of hours at the work site. A Work-Based Learning Contract must be signed by the student, parent/guardian, work-based learning supervisor, school counselor, and principal. There is a quarterly review of the student’s program, and grades are given on a pass/fail basis. Transportation to the work-based learning site is the responsibility of the family.
